lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Hi Tom, thanks for hopping on. Quick note before we start — this call is being recorded for note-taking purposes. Is that alright with you?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Yep, fine by me.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Great. So — three weeks into the trial. How has the team been getting on with it?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Honestly? Better than I expected. The recruiters actually use it, which is more than I can say for the last tool we rolled out.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: That's a low bar, but I'll take it. Anything that hasn't landed well?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: A couple of the senior folks grumbled about learning another tool, but the call summaries won them over pretty quickly. My ops lead pulled the usage numbers yesterday — nineteen of the twenty-four trial seats were active every single week.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Nineteen of twenty-four weekly actives is genuinely strong for a trial. Are the summaries what's saving them time, or is it more the coaching side?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Both, but the time saving is the visible one. My senior recruiters reckon they're getting about forty minutes a day back on call write-ups. That's real.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Forty minutes a day is the number I'd anchor on. What does that translate to in placements, roughly?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Hard to say precisely, but my back-of-envelope is that if each recruiter gets one extra candidate conversation a day out of it, the thing pays for itself several times over.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: That's the math I'd put in front of anyone who asks about the spend.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Look, the product does what you said it would. The question is whether the number works. Let's talk pricing.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Happy to. You've seen list — fifty dollars per seat per month, billed annually. At twenty-four seats that comes to fourteen thousand four hundred a year.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Right, and that's where I need you to sharpen your pencil. Fourteen and a half grand is a big line item for a firm our size. I'm not paying list.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Understood. Before I talk numbers, help me size this properly — is twenty-four the right seat count for the full rollout, or does that grow?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: We're hiring. Realistically we're at twenty-eight, maybe thirty seats by the middle of next year.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Okay, that matters, because I get more room on price as the commitment gets bigger. Two levers there — seat count, or term length. Have you thought about a two-year agreement?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: My default is annual. I've been burned on multi-year software deals before.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: What happened, if you don't mind me asking?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: We signed three years on our old ATS. The product stagnated, support got slower every quarter, and we were stuck paying for it until last spring. I'm not eager to repeat that experience.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: That's fair, and lock-in risk is real. Let me put both options on the table and you can react. On a straight annual at twenty-four seats, I can move from fifty down to forty-six a seat. On a two-year term, I can go to forty-two, and I'll lock that rate for any seats you add, so your new hires come in at the same price.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Forty-six is barely a dent. I'll be straight with you, Priya — we also ran a trial with CallScribe last quarter, and their rep called me last week quoting thirty-five a seat to win us back.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: I appreciate you telling me directly. Can I ask — if CallScribe at thirty-five was the answer, why are we on this call?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Because my recruiters didn't rate it. The transcripts were sloppy and the coaching features felt bolted on. But at a fifteen-dollar gap per seat, I have to at least weigh it.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: That's the right way to weigh it. My honest take: if the transcript layer is sloppy, everything built on top of it is sloppy — summaries, coaching, all of it. Your team already voted with their usage. I'd guess nineteen of twenty-four seats a week is not what CallScribe adoption looked like.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: No. Half the team had quietly stopped using it by week two.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: So the fifteen-dollar gap is only a saving if people actually use the thing.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Fine, point taken. But I still can't take fourteen grand to my managing partner and call it a win. And there's another thing that worries me — the switching effort itself.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Say more?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: We just came off an ATS migration in the spring and the team is running on fumes. Even if we pick you, I can't afford six weeks of setup, integrations, and retraining. What does rollout actually involve?

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Less than you'd think, because you're not starting from zero — your team has been live on it for three weeks already. Going from trial to rollout means turning on the remaining five seats, connecting your ATS, and a forty-five minute admin session for your ops lead. The connector for your ATS is prebuilt. Call it two or three days elapsed, not six weeks.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: And the trial data carries over? Nobody loses their call history?

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Everything carries over. Same workspace, same logins — nothing gets migrated because nothing moves.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Okay. That's less painful than I feared. So back to the number. Give me forty a seat on the annual and we can wrap this up this week.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Forty on a one-year I genuinely can't do — that's below where I'm allowed to go without a longer commitment. Here's my best structure. Annual at forty-four. Or the two-year at forty-two, and on the two-year I'll add a ninety-day performance clause.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: What does the performance clause actually mean?

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: If at day ninety your weekly active usage has dropped below what you saw in the trial, you can exit the second year with sixty days' written notice. It's our way of taking the ATS-contract scenario off the table — if the product stops earning its keep, you're not trapped.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Hm. That takes most of the sting out of the multi-year idea, I'll admit.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: And with your hiring plan, the price lock matters too. At thirty seats next year, forty-two versus list is about a twenty-nine hundred dollar difference annually, and it grows with every hire.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: You've clearly done this before. What about support? Part of the ATS disaster was waiting four days for ticket responses.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Both options include priority support — first response inside four business hours, and you keep me as your named contact rather than going into a queue.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Put that in writing. Alright. I'm not going to say yes today — I don't sign anything this size without my managing partner, and Dana is out until Monday.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Completely reasonable. What would help Dana say yes?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: She'll care about three things: the total cost, the exit clause in plain English, and proof the team actually uses it. The usage report covers the last one.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Then here's what I propose. I'll send you both options in writing by end of day tomorrow — annual at forty-four, and the two-year at forty-two with the ninety-day clause and the price lock on added seats — plus a one-page summary Dana can read in five minutes. Then can we get thirty minutes with you and Dana on Tuesday to walk through it?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Tuesday afternoon works. Send the proposal over and I'll get it in front of her over the weekend.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Done. And so there's no artificial pressure here — I'll hold this pricing through the end of the month. You don't have to decide on the spot Tuesday.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Appreciated. Between us, if Dana is comfortable with the exit clause, the two-year is probably where we land.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Then I'll make sure the clause is airtight and readable. Anything else you need from me before Tuesday?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: One thing — a reference from another recruiting firm around our size would help. Dana likes hearing from peers.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: I'll line one up. There's a fifty-person staffing firm in Denver that moved to us from CallScribe, actually — I'll ask if their ops director will take a call this week.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Perfect. That's everything from my side.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Great. So to recap: proposal with both options by end of day tomorrow, reference intro this week, and thirty minutes Tuesday afternoon with you and Dana. I'll send the calendar invite right after this call.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Sounds good. Talk Tuesday, Priya.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Thanks Tom. Speak then.

follow_up_email.subject: Proposal + Tuesday walkthrough — Open Gong x Meridian Recruiting
follow_up_email.body:
Hi Tom,

Great conversation today — and congrats on those trial numbers. Nineteen of twenty-four seats active every week is the kind of adoption most tools never see.

As promised, you'll have the full proposal by end of day tomorrow with both options:
- Annual: $44/seat/month for 24 seats
- Two-year: $42/seat/month, with the 90-day performance exit clause and a price lock on every seat you add as you hire

I'll include a one-page summary Dana can read in five minutes, with the exit clause spelled out in plain English. I'm also reaching out to the ops director at a Denver staffing firm that moved to us from CallScribe — I'll aim to have that intro ready before we meet.

This pricing holds through the end of the month, so there's no need to decide on the spot Tuesday.

Calendar invite for Tuesday afternoon is on its way. Looking forward to meeting Dana.

Best,
Priya

fields.name: discovery_quality
fields.justification: Priya re-qualified before negotiating: seat growth, term-length appetite, the story behind the multi-year aversion, and Dana's actual decision criteria. She anchored value on the customer's own numbers (40 min/day saved) rather than defending price. Slightly less depth on Meridian's broader goals, but this was a negotiation call, not discovery.

evidence.quote: is twenty-four the right seat count for the full rollout, or does that grow?
What would help Dana say yes?

fields.name: objection_handling
fields.justification: Every objection was met on the merits: the CallScribe price gap was reframed around adoption using Tom's own trial data, the lock-in fear was answered with a concrete 90-day performance exit clause, and the switching-cost worry was dissolved with a specific two-to-three-day rollout scope. Priya conceded on price only in exchange for commitment, and removed pressure by holding pricing through month end.
